sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Agent memory is context management, not one store
sections.para: Against the industry's single similarity store, memory here is context management: many memories, fractal by altitude, published and open, and shared through vaults. The evidence is one Claude Code session that, across several context resets, revised an article, wrote two more, published a vault and shipped six releases in a day.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Memory is work: many sourced, fractal, shared memories
sections.para: Memory means deciding what an agent needs in its window now, the question the industry calls context engineering. It is many memories with their own vocabularies, fractal from principles to code, published openly, shared through vaults, and carries provenance on every item. Stale pages become false memories: four found, two fixed.

sections.label: Memory is not a spectator sport
sections.line: One passive store that holds everything is wrong
sections.para: The camera picture of memory is wrong three ways. There should not be one store, because context is specific and the twenty-seven sites, forty vaults, CRM and inbox are rightly inconsistent. It should not hold everything, because context costs tokens and attention. And it should not be passive, because memory is made deliberately.

sections.label: What the industry built, and where we agree
sections.line: The industry has arrived at files and context budgets
sections.para: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini offer vendor-held memory of conversations. MemGPT, Letta, Mem0 and Zep are more interesting, and Letta found a plain filesystem scored 74.0 percent on LoCoMo against 68.5 for Mem0's graph. Manus, Anthropic's memory tool and Karpathy's context engineering all point to files and the window as the scarce thing.

sections.label: Memory is context management
sections.line: Agentic sessions and one-shot calls need memory with altitudes
sections.para: Agentic sessions load memory a little at a time and compact; one-shot calls need a small bundle that is right first time. Both work if memory has altitudes: llms.txt at about 106 kilobytes, all article graphs at 234, one graph at eight, an article around sixty, a vault bundle a megabyte.

sections.label: Many memories, each its own context
sections.line: Each site, vault, inbox and CRM is a memory
sections.para: Sites hold principles, the release log 211 entries, vaults forty worked examples totalling 328 megabytes, Email-FS the inbox conversations, and the CRM a world per contact. Each keeps its own ontology; links and an index join them, not a schema. Openness makes the memory usable: public pages can be fetched, quoted and cited.

sections.label: Provenance built in
sections.line: Every item carries its source, so nothing needs trusting
sections.para: Shared memory made by agents needs provenance or becomes a rumour mill, and context rot makes long windows unreliable. Here every quote has a URL, every release a commit hash, every vault a read key, every source file a hash and every page a byline. A similarity score is not a source.

sections.label: What it looked like in the session that wrote this
sections.line: The writing session remembered only what its files remembered
sections.para: The session ran for days across context resets, carrying only a summary. It read by altitude, used research agents and another team's review vault, checked every number against reality and wrote back: two articles with graphs, a vault, and six release log entries including its mistakes.

sections.label: The loop, and the conventions that keep it cheap
sections.line: The loop of publish, index, load, act, write back
sections.para: A memory differs from an archive by its loop: publish, index, load by altitude, act and check, then write back. Conventions matter more than tooling: Email-FS lite mailrooms let a conductor run twelve agents, Issues-FS makes issues folders, and read keys share memory safely. Nothing is remembered by the model between sessions.

sections.label: Where it falls short
sections.line: Stale pages, opinion, discovery and single-estate testing limit it
sections.para: Stale pages become false memories: research found four more, such as 617 nodes against the corrected 1,051 and a 155 KB file that was 2.5 megabytes. Two were fixed. The memory is one person's opinions, discovery is hard at scale, and no second estate has yet tested the thesis.

sections.label: What exists today, and what does not
sections.line: Most of the memory runs; key pieces are missing
sections.para: Running today: the sites and llms.txt indexes, article graphs, the 211-entry release log, forty vaults with read keys, Email-FS lite, Issues-FS, the CRM and session summaries. Missing: a second estate, a build freshness check for stale claims, a published hand-off summary shape, the one-shot bundle vault, and a librarian role on this site.

sections.para: Sources include Anthropic's context engineering and memory tool pages, OpenAI and Google memory announcements, MemGPT, Letta's filesystem benchmark, Mem0, Zep, Manus, Cognition, LangChain, Karpathy via Pure AI, Chroma's context rot and Lost in the middle.
